contemplating to launch a Virtual University Semi-Arid Tropics (VUSAT) to help 
mitigate the effects of drought and improve the livelihoods of vulnerable rural 
communities in India. Similar, partnerships are being sought for launching the 
VUSAT in drought-prone regions of South Asia and Sub Saharan Africa. 
(b) Yes, Sir. The VUSAT work will be initiated in India in the States of Andhra 
Pradesh, Kamataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. In 
each State, a host of key institutions will come together to establish a State-level hub, 
and will proceed to set up rural information centres each one of which will serve a 
number of villages around. 
(c) The aims and objectives of this initiative are as follows :— 
 
1. Educate and train a wide array of stakeholders in the dry tropics about 
drought mitigation, climate management and livelihood opportunities; 
2. Communicate relevant and timely information for community 
mobilization to mitigate the impact of drought; and 
3. Establish and sustain a virtual network of policy makers, 
researchers, educators, service providers and farm communities 
towards effective drought mitigation and climate management. 
(d) and (e) The feasibility study  for ihe VUSAT was prepared

*504. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA : Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is a price control on imported 
formulations also; 
(b) what is Government's policy and which are the products that have been 
granted price approval of import of formulations; 
8 

[25 April, 2003] RAJYASABHA 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Ely Lilly, Nicholas, Aventis have flouted 
the DPCO fully in case of finished fo rmulations prices; if so, the details 
thereof; and 
(d) whether it is also a fact that these cases have been referred to CBI 
for further probe? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SUKH 
DEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Prices of scheduled imported formulations are fixed as per 
para 7 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995, by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) . Para 7 provides that the landed 
cost shall form the basis for fixing its price alongwith such margin to cover 
selling and distribution expenses including interest and importer's profit which 
shall not exceed fifty per cent of the landed cost. Importers of non-Scheduled 
formulations fix their price on their own as per cost of import and prevailing 
market competition etc. NPPA regularly examines the movement in prices of 
non-scheduled formulations (including imported formulations) on the basis of 
information available to it from various sources. 
(c) and (d) No case of flouting Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
provisions/price violation in case of finished formulation prices has come to 
the notice of National Phar maceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) in respect of 
M/s Ely Lilly, M/s Nicholas and M/s Aventis. However, a technical fault in the 
prices charged by M/s Aventis Pharma Limited for two imported Insulin 
formulations came to the notice of NPPA . This has not been referred to CBI 
for further probe.

Utilisation of funds given for Yamuna Action Plan 
*506. SHRIS. S. AHLUWALIA : Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the reports in the 
media highlighting continuous rise in the pollution level in the River Yamuna 
despite huge outlay of Rs. 600 crore incurred on the Yamuna Action Plan (YAP): 
(b) if so. Government's comments about the veracity of the report. 
(c) measures taken by Government to ensure judicious utilisation of the 
fund so received from the Japanese Government; and 
(d) the reasons for continuous deterioration of pollution and non 
availability of cleaner water in the river even after huge investment for this 
purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) Under the Yamuna Action Plan, Phase-I of Government 
which has been funded by the Japan Bank for International Co-operation a total 
expenditure of Rs. 668 crore has been incurred on pollution abatement works in 
Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh. Major works implemented under the plan 
are:— 
Sewerage —      170kms. 
Main Pumping Stations —     60 nos. 
Sewage treatment plants        —     32 nos. (734 mid) 
Community Toilets —     1123 nos. (out of which 960 toilet 
complexes have been constructed in 
Delhi) 
In addition, the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi has 
also taken up the work of construction of sewage treatment plants at 17 locations. 
Despite these works, the water quality of Yamuna has not shown appreciable 
improvement along Delhi due to the following reasons : 
(i) As against the present sewage generation of 3300 mid, the installed 
sewage treatment capacity is 2300 mid. Thus, there is a gap of 1000 
mid in the sewage treatment capacity. 
3 9 

RAJYA SABHA [25 April, 2003] 
(ii) Out of about 130 km. length of trunk sewer, about 90 km. length 
requires refurbishing and rehab ilitation as the sewers are either 
silted up or settled. As a result, the installed capacity of sewage 
treatment plant is not fully utili zed and the untreated sewage is 
discharged in the river through various drains. 
(iii) Out of a total of  15 common effluent treatment plants to be 
constructed in 21 industrial estates, only 3 have been completed so 
far. The remaining ones are targeted for completion by December, 
2003. 
(iv) Lack of dilution capacity in the river particularly along Delhi. 
Some of the major works of construction of additional sewage treatment 
plants and refurbishing and rehabilitation of trunk sewers have been included 
in the Yamuna Action Plan Phase-II. In addition, the National Capital Territory 
of Delhi has also taken up the work of construction of two large Sewage 
Treatment Plants. All the riparian states of Yamuna except Delhi have also 
agreed to release their share in the minimum flow of fresh water of 10 cubic 
metres per second along the Delhi stretch of the river. Government of National 
Capital Territory of Delhi has expressed its inability lo release its share of 
minimum flow which is 4.6%. due to shortage of drinking water in Delhi. 
The implementation of river cleaning programme is reviewed by both the 
Govt, oflndia and the State Govt, at various levels regularly. Funds are released 
to the Implementing Agencies of the St ate Governments only after the receipt 
of proper utilization certificates authenticated by competent authorities.

Conversion of waste plastic into fuels 
*519. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that a Nagpur based Scientist has successfully 
invented a unique process converting waste plastic into fuels: 
(b) if so, the salient features thereof; and 
(c) whether this invented fuel is environment friendly? 
THE MINISTER FOR ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) As per the informa tion available. Professor Alka Umesh 
Zadgaonkar. Head of the Department of Applied Chemistry in GH Raisoni College 
of Engineering, Nagpur has worked out a process for conversion of waste plastic 
into fuels. The salient process features include : 
• Feeding of shredded plastic waste into a reactor. 
• When the shredded plastic is heat ed at 350 degree centigrade in 
the presence of a catalyst it forms a mixed fuel. 
• In the second stage when the mixed fuel is subjected to fractional 
distillation it forms petrol (50%) kerosene (20%) diesel (25%) and 
lubricating oil (5%). 
The liquid fuel obtained from this process is stated to contain insignificant 
concentrations of sulphur and nitrogen, which is comparable with natural gasoline 
in its quality parameters.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV) : (a) Government of India have formulated a 
comprehensive National Agriculture Policy in July, 2000. It includes policy for rainfed 
farming in the country. 
(b) The National Agriculture Policy, 2000. as it pertains to rainfed farming, 
provides : 
• Integrated and holistic development of rainfed areas will be promoted by 
conservation of rain water by vegetative measures on watershed basis and 
augmentation of biomass production through agro and farm forestry with the 
involvement of the watershed community.

lines will be treated as one geo-hydrological entity. 
• Management of grazing land will receive greater attention for augmenting 
availability of animal feed and fodder.

Decaying Mahabodhi tree 
3781. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR : W ill the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government's attention has been drawn to the news that 
appeared in media regarding Mahabodhi tree facing pest threat; and 
(b) the curative measures Government propose to take to prevent further 
deterioration of tree? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI DHJP SINGH JUDEV): (a) and(b) Yes. Sir The following measures 
have been taken to protect the tree from the attack of pest and decay : 
(i) Removal of loose bark from the main trunk of the Bodhi Tree through sharp 
sickle/kharpi. 
(ii) Application of Boardeaux mixture (1 : 1 : 10) on the trunk and the 
branches through brush. 
(iii) Fortnightly spraying of the mixture of Vapone (1 millilitre/Utre of water) and 
Sandovit (1/2 millilitre/litre of water) for pest control and Multiplex to supplement 
the nutrients. 
(iv) Removal of weeds from the adjacent lawns situated on the western side of 
the Bodhi Tree. 
(v) The pulverization of the soil of the lawn with the help of spade and 
application of 2 kg. of Potassium Sulphate, 5kg. of Single Superphosphate and 30 kg. 
of Neem cake. 
(vi) Gradual pruning of excess growth of branches on annual basis in the 
presence of a Horticulture Expert and painting of the cut portion with Bordeaux paste. 
(vii) Providing sufficient irrigation through pits dug in the lawns adjacent to the 
Bodhi Tree. 
(viii) Regular monitoring through the Bodh Gaya Temple Management 
Committee under the Chairmanship of the District Magistrate, Gaya.

programme; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ASHOK PRADHAN) : (a) The 
Government has    sanctioned 59703 posts of new teachers under 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [25 April, 2003] 
Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. The State Governments have been advised to recruit 
at least 50% woman teachers under the programme. 
(b) All States and UTs, except Goa, Andaman & Nicobar, Chandigarh, 
Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu who had not submitted their District 
Plans for 2002-03, are covered under this Programme. 
(c) The Scheme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan has been launched by the 
Government to pursue universal elementary education in a mission mode in 
partnership with States. 
The programme is being implemented through State Level Societies, 
with the funding being shared between the Central Government and the State 
Government in the ratio of 85:15 in the Ninth Plan, 75 : 25 in the Tenth Plan 
and 50 : 50 thereafter. 
The programme covers the entire country and addresses the needs of 
192 million children in 11 lakh habitations. 8.5 lakh existing primary and upper 
primary school and 33 lakh existing teachers would be covered under the 
Scheme. The programme seeks to open new schools in habitations which do 
not have schooling facilities and strengthen existing school infrastructure 
through provision of additional class rooms, toilets, drinking water, 
maintenance grant and school improveme nt grant. Existing schools with 
inadequate teacher strength would be provided additional teachers under the 
programme. The capacity of existing teachers would be built by extensive 
training, provision of grant for deve loping teaching-learning material and 
development of academic su pport structure. SSA has a special focus on girls 
and children of weaker sections. A nu mber of initiatives, including free 
textbooks, target these children unde r the programme. SSA also seeks to 
provide computer education even in rural areas to bridge the digital divide. 
The programme envisages the prepar ation of District Elementary 
Education Plans by the States reflecting community based habitation and 
village level planning. These Plans are appraised by teams constituted for the 
purpose, including representatives of the State Government. Based on the 
recommendation of the Appraisal Team, funds are released in terms of SSA 
norms.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR.  VALLABHBHAI RAMJIBHAI 
KATHIRIA) : (a) As per the Memorandum of Association, the objectives of 
the National Book Trust, India are as follows : 
(0 to produce and to encourage the production of good literature, and to 
make such literature available at moderate prices to the public; 
(ii) in furtherance of the above objectives to published more particularly 
books of the following types in'English, Hindi and other languages

3856.   SHRIRUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA : 
SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO : 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: 
Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that bananas may face extinction within ten years 
on account of pests and diseases; and 
(b) if so, the genetic engineering efforts proposed to save bananas from 
going extinct? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY 
(SHRI BACH1 SINGH RAWAT) : (a) and (b) As per the report in an 
international journal, New Scientist (J anuary, 2003), a leading researcher has 
stated that banana could be wiped out by two diseases, namely, Panama 
disease and Black Sigatoka, that have struck Africa, South America and Asia. 
However the reports by American Phytopathological Society (APS) and UN 
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) state that banana is not on the 
verge of extinction since it is unlikely that these diseases will prove fatal. 
These diseases can be controlled throug h use of fungicides and pesticides. In 
addition, use of germplasm of greater genetic diversity for plantation and 
developing genetically engineered disease resistant plants will also help in 
tackling this problem.Studies on genetic engineering and genomics are 
underway in many research laboratories in India and abroad. 
So far, there is no risk of extinction of Banana in India because bananas 
are cultivated under polyclonal system , whereas it is grown as monoclonal 
system in Latin America and Caribbean countries. India harbours a wide range 
of banana varieties; some of which constitute a valuable gene pool to be used 
to develop resistance to major pests and diseases for use in developing 
improved varieities.

THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI VIKRAM 
VERMA) : (a) to (c) "Sports" is a State subject and it is primarily the 
responsibility of the State Government to create sports facilities at various 
places, including hilly and rural areas, to promote sports at all levels. However, 
in order to supplement the efforts of the State Governments in this direction, 
Central assistance is provided to the State Governments/Municipal 
corporations/schools etc. for creati on of various sports facilities under the 
Scheme of Grants for Creation of Sports  Infrastructure, subject to the receipt 
of viable proposals from the States. For construction of sports projects in 
hilly areas, Central assistance is provided on 75:25 basis between the Central 
Government and the State Government against 50:50 basis for other areas.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Diversion of funds by NTC in Pondicherry 
SHRI OP. THIRUNAVUKKARASU (P ONDICHERRY): The National 
Textiles Corporation is operating the Swadeshi Cotton Mill in Pondicherry. 
The Mill is functioning as a nationalis ed unit since 1985. The Centre has 
invested corpus fund in the Mill through the National Textiles Corporation. 
Now it has 10,588 spindles and 242 workers. The Mill has suffered a heavy 
loss due to the hike in the price of inputs, stiff competition in the textile market 
and also in designs in the textile business. The Centre introduced the 
Voluntary Retirement Scheme to rehabili tate the Mill in September, 2000. Till 
March, 2002, 174 employees availed of the scheme. 
223 

RAJYA SABHA [25 April, 2003] 
The Mill sold about 9.91 acres of land for Rs. 12 crores. The 
remaining eight acres of land is still av ailable. The sale proceeds of the land 
should be utilised for the workers who are going on VRS, for Provident Fund, 
for the ESI Scheme and for the benefit of the Mill. The National Textiles 
Corporation should not deviate at any stage and divert funds for other 
corporations which are outside Pondic herry. The Government of India should 
intervene in the matter and save the Swadeshi Cotton Mill in Pondicherry.   
Thank you. 
Demand for reservation for OBCs in Tripura 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR (Tripura):- As the highest limit of 50 per 
cent reservation has already been pr ovided to the Scheduled Caste and 
Scheduled Tribe people, ex-servicemen and the physically handicapped 
people, reservation facilities cannot be extended to OBCs on account of the 
Supreme Court's verdict in the case of Indira Sawhney and others versus the 
Union Government of India. As such the OBC people of Tripura have been 
remaining out^ of the reservation facilit ies in the State level services. Removal 
of this hurdle is beyond the capacity of the State Government. 
In this situation, I would urge upon the Government of India to come 
forward to remove the legal barrier in Tripura, if necessary, by amending the 
law and apply this principle to other Stat es also where reservation for OBCs is 
not in force for the same reason. Thank you.

Need to bring legislation to facilitate linking of rivers 
SHRI C.PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): The National Water Development 
Agency was set up in 1982 to carry out detailed studies, surveys and 
investigations and to prepare feasibilit y reports on linking of rivers in the 
country. This Agency has identified 30 links for preparation of feasibility 
reports and has prepared feasibility reports of 6 such links. A Task Force was' 
set up in December, 2002, to co-ordinate among the States and to provide 
guidance on norms of appraisal of individual projects. According to reports, 
Action Plan I and II should be ready by the end of July this year. It is the duty 
of the Centre to take necessary steps for the early completion of work and to 
see that water scarce States, like Tamil Na du, get their due. Therefore, it is 
necessary to bring forward a legislation for nationalising rivers. Then alone, 
redirecting surplus water to water-sca rce States could be effectively done 
through linking rivers. It is also necessary to appoint one member from the 
water-scarce State, Tamil Nadu, to the Task Force. The National Water 
Development Council has assessed the water deficit in Tamil Nadu as 250 
TMC. But, only two, out of the 30 proposed links, will carry water to Tamil 
Nadu. That water will also be insufficient for the State. For example, Cauvery 
is to get only 56.5 TMC water through linkage. The Government of Tamil Nadu 
had apprised the Task Force of the grou nd realities  and  pointed out  the 
need to continue with the  existing  water

RAJYA SABHA [25 April, 2003] 
sharing agreements.    So,  I appeal to the Government to bring forward a 
legislation to nationalise rivers to make linking of rivers a reality. 
Need for installation of Da Vinci Surgical System in all major hospitals in the 
country for by pass surgery 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, open-
heart surgery is traumatic because it re quires a large incision in the chest, 
sawing through the breastbone and then cracking open the ribcage. According 
to the reports, lakhs and lakhs of people in India die annually due to heart 
attacks. But, with the help of Da Vinci, which is a robotic machine, the bypass 
surgery is less painful; it reduces the costs and the chance of infection, 
drastically cuts down the recuperation time, reduces time and causes less 
damage to the surrounding tissues. This is the latest technology that is 
available in the world for bypass surgery. Using Da Vinci not only reduces 
hospitalisation time but it also dispenses with the heart-lung machine which 
takes over the heart's functions when th e heart is stopped in the conventional 
surgery, which is very risky. With the he lp of Da Vinci, a robotic machine, the 
doctor makes only three tiny holes on the left side of the chest. Then, with the 
help of a pair of joysticks,  the surgeon controls the Da Vinci's robotic arms. 
These robotic arms can also reach thos e places which a doctor's arm cannot 
reach. The computer interface mimics  the surgeon's movements on the hand 
and foot controls to a micro millimeter level. So, I strongly suggest for 
installation of Da Vinci, to being with , in all the major Government hospitals 
engaged in by pass surgery in India since the machine costs less than Rs.5 
crores. I hope the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare will take keen interest 
in this and react quickly to my suggestion because it concerns us all. 
Madam, I request you also to re commend it to the Government 
because this is a very important advanced technology.

Postponement of recovery of loans from farmers in Gujarat due to drought 
SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ (Gujarat): Madam, this year, in about 12 
States of the country, ther e have been acute drought and scarcity conditions. 
The nationalised and cooperative banks have postponed the recovery of loans 
and interest in Rajasthan and other States. In Gujarat, in 18 out of 25 districts, 
there are acute drought conditions. Thousands of villages have been declared 
to be facing scarcity conditions by the Gujarat State Government, and various 
relief works have been undertaken, including the setting up of many cattle 
camps. The Central Government has al so given financial assistance to the 
Gujarat State for carrying out the relief work. A special team of the Ministry of 
Agriculture had also visited the scarcit y areas of Gujarat.  Despite that, the 
Government has still not issued the orders for the postponement of the 
recovery of loans an d interest by the said banks. The said banks are taking 
legal steps and adopting coercive measures, either directly or through the 
courts. 
It is, therefore, necessary, in view  of the pitiable condition of the 
loanee farmers, that the Government of India gives instructions to such banks 
for the postponement of the recovery of loans for, at least, one year.

Need for Central assistance for welfare of Backward Classes in Rajasthan 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasth an;: Madam, the Ministry of 
Social Justice and Empowerment, Gove rnment of India had provided Rs.25-
30 crores as Special Central Assistance under the Special Component Plan to 
the State Government of Rajasthan for the welfare of the Scheduled Castes. 
Nearly 65000-70000 families had benefited  by this assistance every year 
through the various programmes cond ucted by the Rajasthan Scheduled 
Castes & Scheduled Tribes Finance and Development Cooperative 
Corporation. For helping the BPL families in crossing over the poverty line and 
attaining economic independence, the Ministry of Rural Development had 
raised the amount of subsidy from  Rs.6000 to Rs. 10000. Since the 
RSCSTFDCC implements programmes on similar patterns as implemented by 
the Rural Development Department, the State Government needs Rs. 70-80 
crores per annum to benefit nearly 85000 BPL families. 
The Government of India insists on regular implementation of 
schemes like Pre-matric Scholarships, Post-matric scholarships, Construction 
of Hostels for SCs, STs and OBC Students.  For construction of  hostels, the 
Central Government provides for 50 per  cent of the expenses. Even if a 
minimum of two hostels, one for boys and one for girls, were to be 
constructed in all the districts of Raja sthan, with a minimum capacity of 25 
students each, the total cost would come  to Rs. 12.80 crores, and the States 
share would be Rs.6.40 crores. However, the State cannot bear the additional 
burden of Rs.42 crores per annum for scholarship programmes. This must 
fully be provided by the Central Government. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Government  to consider the two proposals 
mentioned above for the welfare -- in the true sense -- of the backward 
classes in the State of Rajasthan.

SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR (Punjab): Mr. Vi ce-Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
add my few words in support of the Bill moved by my esteemed friend, Shri 
Santosh Bagrodia. Of all the gains of India's freedom -- there are many of 
them of which we can be justly proud -- our constitutional right, Right to 
Liberty and Freedom, is our pre-eminent claim to glory as a democracy. In a 
way, this Bill has drawn attention to the infraction of our valuable constitutional 
right, right to privacy, which by a se ries of pronouncements by the Supreme 
Court, has been read as an integral co mponent of the right guaranteed by 
article 21 of the Constitution. If the right to privacy were not to be there, or, if 
we were to permit insidious encroachments on that right, our democracy, our 
democratic way of life, the liberty of our citizens would have never been the 
one that the founding fathers of our Cons titution had intended to guarantee to 
the citizens of free India. Sir, over the past few years, we have seen the State 
assuming wide powers in the name of security of the State, in the name of the 
law and order, in the name of combati ng certain evils. They certainly do need 
to be checked and curtailed. But whether the powers assumed by the State, in 
the name of such compelling circumstanc es, have, in fact, been used for the 
purpose for which these powers had been assumed, is the question that we 
are, today, debating in the form of this Bill. As far back as 1997, the People's 
Union for Civil Liberty brought a case before the Supreme Court that 
concerned itself with unchecked recording of telephonic conversation of the 
citizens of this country. It was pointed out that despite the Indian Telegraph 
Act conferring powers upon the Government to make regulations to check the 
abuse of such interceptions, no rules, no regulations were forthcoming; and, 
the Supreme Court was compelled to issue certain directions. I call the 
attention of the hon. Minister to those regulations. One of the guidelines given 
by the apex court was that except with the prior permission of the Union or the 
State Home Secretary, which could be delegated to the Joint Secretary also, 
there would be no interception of telephonic conversation. 
Sir, I ask the Minister of this question whether this salutary 
safeguard has, in fact, been observed. I can say so from personal knowledge, 
Sir, that these safeguards still continue to be in realm of theory

and not practised in the realm of day- to-day existence. With the private 
telecom operators now entering the fray of telecommunications, they informed 
me that all that they are told by t he concerned Ministry is that 'X' numbers 
have to be checked and tapped, and we have no option but to comply with 
those directions. Sir, this is a seriou s matter. It impinges upon the privacy of 
the home, it impinges upon the dignity of  the individual, and it also concerns 
itself with the abuse of extraordinary po wers that have been given to the State 
only to meet the most compelling situat ions; on an emergent si tuation, in the 
national interest, and in the interest of national security. Sir, the right to 
privacy, in philosophical terms, in terms of our constitutional jurisprudence, is a 
right to be left alone. When you say that the right to privacy means a right to 
be left alone, it means no more than sayi ng that in one's day-to-day existence 
do not encroach upon, what an Englishman called, the privacy of his home, 
that is, the privacy of his castle. A hom e is one's castle where a man can live 
the way he is, not the way he would like the world to know him. It -means that 
is a place where a man, actually, expr esses the autonomy of his person with 
all his weaknesses, with all his preferences, and with all his prejudices, and 
with all his habits. I feel, Sir, this is something that goes to the dignity of the 
individual-, it is one of t he most basic human right that a free citizen in a free 
country like India must be allowed to enj oy unhindered. Sir, the Bill seeks to 
introduce necessary safeguards against the infraction of the privacy of the 
home. And I commend Shri Bagrodiaji for drawing the attention of this House 
to this right, which right, although implicit in article 21, implicit in article 19 (1) 
(a), implicit in a democratic way of life, implicit in our traditions, is yet not safe 
from encroachments. These encroachments are never unconscious; that is the 
worst part of it, Sir. The encroachments on the right to privacy are conscious 
encroachments; they are deliberat e encroachments, and encroachments 
justified in the name of the law. And I dar e to say, Sir, that  no law that offends 
the basic structure of the Constitution, of which article 21 is a part, can ever be 
justified in the name of law. All law, all legislation, must be subordinated to this 
primary duty to protect our privacy, to pr otect our individuality. And, Sir, in a 
nation of one billion people, if there ar e 50, 100, 200 people who need to be 
checked, does not justify sweeping powers, whose use is unhindered by any 
regulation, by any rule that effectively prevents the abuse of  that power. That 
is my first submission, Sir. 
Sir, I would put forward my second submission, and then, I would 
conclude.   Sir, my second submission is that technological advances, today,

DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA (Assam): Mr. Vice Chairman, Sir, I 
thank you for giving me an opportunity to speak on the issue brought to this 
House, through the Private Members' Bill by Shri Santosh Bagrodiaji. Sir, this 
issue is very important under the pr esent circumstances and I am in full 
support of it, to insert a clause ma king the privacy as a part of our 
fundamental right. 
Sir, the usual reply of the Governm ent will be that our Constitution 
provides full guarantee to the citizens for their life and property. In fact, our 
Constitution is foolproof in all respec ts, but there is only one problem. The 
problem is some exceptions are there. Whenever some exceptions are 
provided to be applicable under extraordinary' circumstances, the 
extraordinary circumstances become the general one, totally undermining the 
objectives for which certain provisions, either in the Constitution, or, in the law, 
were framed. That is the situation that in the inde pendent country where we 
must have all freedom for life and property  and a dignified life, there is always 
interference. The existing provisions hav e failed to give us that protection. 
What is the remedy? Sir, I do not want  to repeat many of the instances and 
good arguments put forward by my colleagues who have spoken earlier. But, I 
want to cite one or two examples to justify why this privacy should be very 
drastically applied as a part of our fundamental right. 
I was an active member of the All Assam Students Union when the 
Assam agitation on foreigners' issue was taking place for six years. I was in a 
hostel. There were raids in the hostel for more than 64 times and on an 
average all the students were taken out to the streets. 
Almost all the hostels were raided. One night, the police took me out 
of my room and after two or three minutes they came back with a paper and 
asked me to sign that paper. It was wri tten on the paper that some detonators 
were found under my pillow. I was forced to sign that paper. Then a message 
was flashed that Mr. Sarma had links with insurgent and terrorist groups. It 
was done to malign my image. A case was filed against me so that I was 
dissociated with the agitation. It was a de mocratic agitation. There is a rule 
that every raid party should be accompanied by a Magistrate and the house 
should be raided in the presence of the ow ner of the house. But, ih reality it 
never happens. The police is free to file any case. As has been rightly pointed 
out by my colleagues, the police always  presume that the person whom they 
are going

to arrest is a criminal, even if he is an innocent person. They have pre-
connotations. Irrespective of the fact whether the person is criminal or not, he 
is treated as a criminal and charges are framed against him as a criminal. 
There is no remedy. The situation is very pathetic in the insurgency prone 
areas. I also represent one such area. Jammu and Kashmir is also having the 
same problem. In these areas, the Army and the police have been given free 
hand to do whatever they want to do. If they come to know that some

bring the entire population of the villa ge in the open field and it is normally 
done in the night time, after 12 o' clock. All the people are subjected to a lot of 
harassment for the whole night. They never care for any person, whether they 
are men or women, whether he is a hear t patient or he is a baby of two or 
three months old, or he is a student wh o has to appear for an exam the next 
day. They bring them out irrespective of  their ages. Sir, there is an instance 
that a very respectable person was forced to respond to the nature's call in 
public. This is the society where we live in! If we don't impose certain 
restrictions or some penalty, as rightly pointed out by some of my colleagues, 
on the officers or persons who are respons ible for infringement of the right to

When the Minister replies to the debate, probably it would be a routine reply. I

these areas, the Army and the police ha ve been given so much freedom that

take out the ornaments, money and other valuable things and they don't put it 
on record. That is why their greed is increasing day by day. They have made it 
a habit to raid houses in posh colonies. This has become another problem in 
certain insurgency-prone areas. We must give a serious thought to this 
particular issue. If some nuisance is created, there is a provision for imposing

some party is going on, they will make a lot of noise by singing and dancing

There is no privacy. If I want to sleep at night, because I cannot

SHRI G.K. VASAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I thank you for giving me an 
opportunity to speak on this important  Bill. India is a democratic country, and 
all its citizens have a right to express their views and to maintain their privacy. 
Privacy is the main part of a life of an y person. Personal privacy is a right and 
it should be protected and maintained. The Government should play an 
important part in protecting the privacy of the common people, political people, 
or, persons who are famous in the c ountry in any field. Privacy means 
security. Privacy should be disturbed only when there is a threat to national 
security from that person. There are many ways of disturbing the right of 
privacy, for example, through robbery,  -blackmailing, dacoity, or, by carrying 
out terrorists activities, etc. These are totally punishable by law, and are 
carried out against the will of anybody in  the country. Any kind of punishment, 
any rigorous punishment, can be given to  these kinds of persons who disturb 
the privacy of a person. The other way of disturbing privacy is, politically, when 
the Government disturbs the right of the privacy; you may call it political anger 
or vendetta. This is slowly becoming a practice. In our country, a lot of such 
examples can be given, politically and officially. Princess Diana's death in a 
car accident is a typical case of dist urbing, her privacy. She lost her life 
because of disturbance to her privacy. Politically when a person is in power 
and tries to show political anger against the Opposition, this is another kind of 
disturbance of privacy. When the Government shows anger against 
journalists, who do not give opinion in its favour; this is another kind of 
disturbance to privacy. When officials try to show vendetta against common 
persons for personal reasons, and, also use police role against public, these 
are all different kinds of disturbing t he privacy of a person. These are very 
easy ways to disturb the privacy of a pe rson. I would also like to request the 
media to play a very correct and proper role in maintaining the right of privacy 
of the people. For example, misusing authority for publicity, for creating 
sensational news, should be banned and everybody has to be aware of it 
because it disturbs the right  of privacy of a person. The media has got to play 
a very important role in this, because the media can go even to the bedroom 
of a common
